From Breaking Plates To Crossing 7 Waves: Unusual New Year Traditions From Around The World
Curated By :
Last Updated:
While fireworks and parties may be universal, many countries mark the turning of the calendar with customs that are as unusual as they are meaningful
1/6
As the final seconds of the year slip away and midnight sweeps across the globe, the celebration of the New Year unfolds in countless colours, sounds and rituals. In Spain, the stroke of midnight signals not just the beginning of another year but also the start of a race against the clock. Revelers gather with bowls of grapes and attempt to swallow twelve of them in rhythm with the twelve chimes that ring in the year. Each grape, locals say, represents good fortune for one of the twelve months ahead. Those who manage to keep pace with the bells are assured of happiness. (AI-Generated Image)
2/6
Denmark greets the year with a rather noisier ritual. Throughout New Year's Eve, old plates and cups are hurled at the doorsteps of friends and family. By morning, the pile of shattered crockery outside a home becomes an unusual symbol of affection. The more broken china you find, the more loved, and luckier, you are believed to be. (AI-Generated Image)
ADVERTISEMENT
3/6
In Japan, the soundscape of New Year's Eve is dominated not by fireworks but by the slow, echoing toll of temple bells. Buddhist temples ring their bells 108 times, a number that symbolises the earthly desires and human weaknesses that cause suffering. With each resonant strike, worshippers believe one worldly sin is purified, allowing the New Year to begin with a clear and peaceful mind. (AI-Generated Image)
4/6
Scotland's Hogmanay celebrations come with a tradition known as "first footing". As the clock ushers in the New Year, the identity of the first person to cross a home’s threshold is said to determine the household's luck for the coming year. A visitor arriving with symbolic gifts, such as coal, once linked to warmth and prosperity, is especially welcome. (AI-Generated Image)
ADVERTISEMENT
5/6
In the Philippines, circles are the shape of fortune. Families decorate homes with round objects, wear polka-dotted clothing and feast on round fruits. The circular forms are believed to represent coins, drawing wealth and prosperity into the household as the year begins. (AI-Generated Image)
6/6
And in Chile, the New Year carries a deeply emotional note in some towns, where families gather not in their living rooms but in cemeteries. Graves are adorned with candles, soft music fills the night air and loved ones sit quietly beside the departed, symbolically sharing the first moments of the year with those they have lost.
